title: Checks, captures, and threats
objectives: Before picking a move, scan candidate moves for whether they give check, capture material, or create a threat
Find a check hiding in a position that otherwise looks quiet
Find a capture that isn't the first thing your eye lands on
Recognize that a move can be strong purely because it threatens something next turn, even with no check or capture right now

steps.text: Before you play any move, run through three questions, in order: can I give CHECK? Can I CAPTURE something? Do I (or my opponent) have a THREAT? This is the CCT habit, and it's the foundation for every tactic in this unit. Here, Rxd8+ does two of the three at once — it captures the queen and delivers check. Moves like that are easy to miss if you only look at the first idea that catches your eye.

steps.prompt: The CCT habit means checks matter most, so captures and threats are only worth a quick glance.

feedback.default: All three deserve a real look, in order — not just checks. A quiet threat that isn't a check or a capture can still be the strongest move on the board, because it forces your opponent to spend their next move dealing with it.

steps.successExplanation: Right — check, capture, and threat all deserve a genuine look. A check is just the first thing to rule out, not the only thing that matters.

steps.prompt: You're comparing three candidate moves: one gives check, one wins a pawn, one creates a strong threat but risks nothing right now. Using the CCT habit, which should you actually evaluate?
options: Only the check — checks are forcing, so they're automatically best
All three — checks, captures, and threats each deserve a real look before you decide
Only the move that wins material
Whichever one looks the flashiest on the board

feedback.default: The CCT habit isn't about picking whichever category sounds most important — it's about actually checking all three before you commit to a move, since the strongest move in a position could be any one of them.

steps.successExplanation: Right — the habit is to scan all three every time, then decide which candidate is actually strongest in this position.

steps.prompt: Nothing looks urgent here — but scan for check anyway. Play the move that gives check.

hints.text: Run the CCT check: is there a move that gives check, even though nothing is under attack right now?
Look at your rook's file — it lines up with the king's rank if it slides all the way up.
Ra8 delivers check along the 8th rank — a move that was there the whole time, just easy to miss if you never asked the question.

feedback.default: That doesn't give check. The CCT habit means actually checking — is there a rook move along a rank or file that lines up with the king?

steps.successExplanation: Ra8+ delivers check. In a position with nothing obviously happening, it's tempting to skip the CCT scan entirely — but the check was there the whole time.

steps.prompt: The bishop on b2 looks far from the action — but scan its diagonal. Is there a capture waiting?

hints.text: Follow the bishop's whole diagonal to the far corner of the board — don't stop looking after the first few squares.
The rook sits at the far end of the bishop's diagonal.
Bxh8 wins the rook — the bishop's diagonal reaches all the way across the board, which is easy to underestimate when the piece looks 'far away.'

feedback.default: That's not the capture. A bishop's diagonal runs the full length of the board when nothing blocks it — trace it all the way to the far corner.

steps.successExplanation: Bxh8 wins the rook for free. A bishop sitting in the corner of the board still commands its entire diagonal — the CCT habit means checking the whole board, not just the squares near the action.

steps.prompt: This move doesn't capture anything and doesn't give check — but scan for threats too. Play the move that puts the black queen in immediate danger.

hints.text: Neither check nor capture is available this move — but the third question, threat, still applies. What can you attack that has nowhere safe to go?
Your rook and the black queen share a file if the rook slides over.
Ra4 attacks the undefended queen along the a-file. It isn't check, and it isn't a capture yet — but it's the strongest move on the board.

feedback.default: That doesn't create a threat against the queen. Line your rook up on the same file as the queen instead.

steps.successExplanation: Ra4 threatens the undefended queen along the a-file. No check, no capture this move — just a threat — and it's still the best move on the board, because Black must spend the next move saving the queen.

steps.prompt: In a real position, you find one candidate move that gives check but achieves nothing else, and a second, quieter move that creates a threat winning a whole piece next turn. What should the CCT habit lead you to do?
options: Always play the check, since checks are forcing
Compare what each move actually accomplishes, and pick the one that's genuinely stronger — even if that's the quiet threat
Ignore both and look for a third option
Play whichever move you saw first

feedback.default: CCT isn't a ranking of which category always wins — it's a checklist to make sure you don't miss any of the three. A pointless check that achieves nothing isn't automatically better than a threat that wins material.

steps.successExplanation: Right — checking all three categories doesn't mean automatically playing whichever one you find first. Compare what each candidate actually accomplishes, then choose.

steps.summary: The CCT habit — checks, captures, threats — is the calculation discipline the rest of this unit builds on. Before playing a candidate move, ask all three questions, even in a position that looks quiet: is there a check I haven't noticed? A capture on a piece that isn't the obvious one? A threat that doesn't win anything this move but forces a response next move? Every tactic in the lessons ahead — forks, pins, skewers, and the rest — is really just a specific, sharper way of answering these same three questions.
